Revised assessment: The statement’s tone remains net negative given the explicit acknowledgement that the coronavirus will weigh on near‑term activity and risks, but the decisive, countercyclical policy response (rate to the ZLB, large‑scale Treasury/MBS purchases, repo operations, discount window easing, and global dollar swap lines) meaningfully tempers that negativity in light of the literature.
- Countercyclical monetary policy dampens fluctuations; at the ZLB, balance‑sheet tools and open‑market purchases of longer‑term bonds/MBS help support market functioning and aggregate demand (monetary policy stance; open market operations in long‑term bonds).
- Credit/financial accelerator insights indicate easing reduces external finance premia and supports investment and spending, especially for bank‑dependent and smaller firms; liquidity and capital buffer measures alleviate loan‑supply shocks tied to bank capital/required reserves (credit view; Oliner & Rudebusch; Gertler & Gilchrist (1994); bank loan supply shocks related to bank capital ratios; discount window and liquidity buffers).
- With market‑based inflation compensation declining and “muted inflation pressures,” expansion is consistent with expectations‑based frameworks (inflation‑forecast targeting per Svensson) to realign expectations toward the symmetric 2% goal, mitigating deflation risk in a potential liquidity trap.

Most important supporting sentence: "The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on economic activity in the near term and pose risks to the economic outlook."
Most important offsetting sentence: "The Federal Reserve is prepared to use its full range of tools to support the flow of credit to households and businesses..."
